title: The Road to Uhud
subtitle: Quraysh's Vengeance, the War Council in Madinah, and the Treachery of Hypocrites
summary: Quraysh setting aside the entire caravan profits to fund a punitive war, assembling three thousand warriors under Abu Sufyan, Al-Abbas's secret warning to Madinah, the council of war where the Prophet respected the youth's consensus, the unbending resolve of wearing armor, the treachery of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, and encampment at the foot of Mount Uhud.

sections.text: The Thirst for Vengeance in Makkah

For a full year following their humiliating defeat at Badr, the aristocracy of Quraysh burned with a single consuming obsession: vengeance. Under the leadership of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, the council of Dar al-Nadwah passed an extraordinary resolution: the entirety of the fifty thousand gold dinars earned from the Syrian caravan was impounded into a dedicated war treasury. No shareholder was permitted to withdraw his profits; every coin was committed solely to raising, equipping, and provisioning a massive punitive army to crush Madinah.

Enlisting tributary Bedouin tribes such as the Ahabish, Quraysh assembled a formidable coalition of three thousand heavily armed warriors, including two hundred cavalry commanded by Khalid ibn al-Walid with Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and seven hundred suits of chainmail. To ensure no warrior fled, fifteen noble women accompanied the army—led by Abu Sufyan's wife, Hind bint Utbah, who burned to avenge her father Utbah and uncle Shaybah—beating tambourines, chanting stirring battle poetry, and inflaming tribal honor.
The vast desert expanses crossed by the Makkan army on their march toward Madinah.
The Intelligence and the Council of War

The Prophet's uncle, Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who remained in Makkah keeping watchful eyes, dispatched a swift courier who rode three hundred miles in three days, delivering a sealed letter warning the Prophet of the approaching horde. When the Makkan army encamped at Aynayn near the northern foot of Mount Uhud, threatening the agricultural fields of the city, the Prophet assembled his companions for consultation (Shura).

The Prophet shared a vision he had witnessed in his sleep: 'I saw cows being slaughtered, and I saw a notch in the tip of my sword, and I saw that I thrust my hand into an impregnable coat of armor.' He interpreted the slaughtered cows as companions who would be martyred, the notch in his sword as an injury to a member of his household, and the armor as the fortified sanctuary of Madinah.

Based on this vision, the Prophet's personal strategic judgment—shared by senior companions and Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul—was to remain inside Madinah, defending the fortified stone compounds and narrow alleyways where cavalry would be useless and every citizen could rain stones from rooftops. However, a passionate majority of young companions, particularly those who had missed the glory of Badr, led by Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, ardently pleaded to march out: 'O Messenger of God, lead us out against our enemies, lest they think we are cowards!'
The Armor of Prophecy and Unbending Leadership

Honoring the consensus of the consultative assembly over his own inclination, the Prophet entered his private quarters and emerged clad for battle in two suits of mail, wearing a helmet and carrying his sword and shield. Seeing him armed, the young companions felt deep remorse for having pressed their view against his preferred strategy, saying: 'O Messenger of God, it was not for us to oppose you; stay in Madinah if you prefer.'
The Prophet replied with unyielding firmness, establishing an immortal lesson in leadership and resolve:

مَا يَنْبَغِي لِنَبِيٍّ إِذَا لَبِسَ لَأْمَتَهُ أَنْ يَضَعَهَا حَتَّى يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ عَدُوِّهِ
'It is not fitting for a prophet, once he has donned his armor, to take it off until God judges between him and his enemy.' (Musnad Ahmad & Sunan al-Darimi)
The majestic red-granite massif of Mount Uhud towering north of Madinah.

The Muslim army of one thousand men set out on Friday afternoon. At Al-Shawt, between Madinah and Uhud, the leader of the hypocrites, Abdullah ibn Ubayy, executed a treacherous desertion. Taking offense that his defensive advice had not been followed, he withdrew with three hundred of his followers, proclaiming: 'He listened to the youths and disobeyed me! Why should we slay ourselves here, O people?'

This sudden betrayal reduced the Muslim ranks to seven hundred steadfast believers, facing an enemy force more than four times their number. Two Ansari clans, Banu Harithah and Banu Salimah, wavered under the shock, but divine grace steadied their resolve, as recorded in Surah Aal-Imran: 'When two factions among you were about to lose heart, yet God was their protector...' (3:122).

The Prophet marched his remaining seven hundred warriors through the orchards of Harithah, skillfully bypassing the enemy patrols, until he reached the base of Mount Uhud at sunrise on Saturday, the seventh of Shawwal. Positioning his forces with the towering mountain behind them, the Prophet surveyed the plains below, where the destiny of the community was about to be tested in fire and blood.
